claims.text: The IBM Research framework for trajectory-informed memory generation has four components: a Trajectory Intelligence Extractor, a Decision Attribution Analyzer, a Contextual Learning Generator, and an Adaptive Memory Retrieval System.
The Decision Attribution Analyzer in the IBM framework identifies which decisions and reasoning steps led to failures, recoveries, or inefficiencies.

The IBM Contextual Learning Generator produces three types of guidance: strategy tips from successful patterns, recovery tips from failure handling, and optimization tips from inefficient but successful executions.
The IBM Adaptive Memory Retrieval System injects relevant learnings into agent prompts based on multi-dimensional similarity.
The IBM framework extracts structured learnings with provenance, in contrast to generic memory systems that store conversational facts in vector databases.
On the AppWorld benchmark, the IBM framework achieved up to 14.3 percentage point gains in scenario goal completion on held-out tasks.
On complex AppWorld tasks, the IBM framework improved scenario goal completion by 28.5 percentage points, a 149% relative increase.
The IBM paper states that an agent that struggles with a particular API authentication flow today will struggle with the same flow tomorrow unless its prompts are manually updated.
The IBM paper gives a recovery-tip example: when checkout fails due to a missing payment method, verify that payment information is configured before retrying.
The IBM paper gives an optimization-tip example: use a single amazon_empty_cart() call instead of looping amazon_remove_from_cart(item_id) to empty a cart.

The IBM paper criticizes rule-based systems as brittle because developers must manually anticipate patterns, and criticizes generic memory systems for lacking causal analysis of which decisions led to failures.

Anthropic describes 'dreaming' as having an agent reflect on logs or transcripts between sessions to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations, inspired by sleep-time compute from Letta and UC Berkeley.

Anthropic describes a memory hierarchy of transcripts, memory notes written by Claude, memory representations such as wikis, and injected context loaded into every session, with dreaming organizing across these layers.
Anthropic frames writing a memory rule as a prediction that the described pattern will be relevant again.

In Anthropic's CL-Bench 1.0 database-question task, Claude is told the correct answer after responding and can record the failure, theorize about what went wrong, test theories, and turn findings into a rule for future answers.
LangChain defines a trace or log as evidence of what happened that becomes memory only when the lesson is converted into context the agent can retrieve on a later run to change its behavior.
LangChain's memory process is to capture traces, analyze traces, and update memory, using LangSmith Observability as trace store, LangSmith Engine as analyzer, and Context Hub as memory store.

LangChain says many of the most visible agent improvements come from procedural memory (instructions, workflows, skills, tool-use rules), for example fixing wrong tool order, wrong subagent delegation, or ignored tone rules.
A survey of LLM agent memory lists reflective self-improvement as one of five mechanism families and names trustworthy reflection and learned forgetting as open challenges.
The survey describes a debugging agent without memory that retries the exact fix that crashed the build the previous Friday, and says memory lets agents avoid repeating costly mistakes.

Machine Learning Mastery recommends importance scoring before writing memory, storing entries with timestamp, confidence, source and tags, and persisting only entries meeting thresholds (example: importance >= 0.6 and confidence >= 0.7).

Machine Learning Mastery warns that poorly built memory creates persistent, hard-to-trace failures, that stale information can cause repeated mistakes, and that storing everything raises cost and makes retrieval noisier.
Machine Learning Mastery warns that giving all agents in a multi-agent system the same shared memory store lets one agent misread notes written for another agent's own use.

Red Hat notes that as context grows models suffer attention errors and 'context rot', and early studies show a mid-sized model with better harness and memory can outperform a larger model lacking them.
Letta's memory blocks have a label, description, value and character limit, which bounds the context window space allocated to each block of in-context memory.
